outcome: The general finite lattice representation problem (does every finite lattice occur as the congruence lattice of a finite algebra?) remains open, but the last outstanding case among lattices with at most seven elements — the lattice called L7 in DeMeo's 2012 thesis and L10 in the still-unpublished DeMeo–Freese–Jipsen manuscript 'Representing Finite Lattices as Congruence Lattices of Finite Algebras' — was closed in late August/September 2026: Chenxiao Tian posted a note (28 August 2026) representing it as the subgroup interval [S3, PSL(2,64)], which the DeMeo–Freese–Jipsen project team then independently verified by recomputation in GAP and by an independent isomorphism test in the agda-algebras library, and improved with a smaller representation as an interval in Sp(6,2) (index 34560, found by scanning GAP's TomLib).

ai.basis_quote: Commit messages on the verification/tooling pull requests (fin-lat-rep PR #32, and per search results also fin-lat-rep-gap PR #2) read '🤖 AI-assisted development: Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic)' and, on an earlier commit, 'Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic)'; Copilot's automated code review flagged parser bugs, input-validation gaps and test-coverage issues on those same PRs, which the human author then fixed.

disputes.summary: Tian's PSL(2,64)/S3 interval (index 43680) is the published discovery that closes the case, but the fin-lat-rep project subsequently found a smaller representation via Sp(6,2) acting on 34560 points. Issue #33 explicitly frames this as an open 'decision needed' about which representation should lead in the writeup and how credit should be split, and notes the minimal possible representation may still be far smaller (between 16 and 34560 elements).

summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks the general question (posed by Grätzer–Schmidt in 1963 and shown by Pálfy–Pudlák in 1980 to be equivalent to a question about subgroup-lattice intervals in finite groups): is EVERY finite lattice a congruence lattice of a finite algebra? That general question is still open — no resolution, partial or otherwise, of the unrestricted conjecture was found. However, a well-documented and, on the evidence available, genuine case of the problem was settled within the window: DeMeo, Freese and Jipsen's manuscript on representing all lattices with at most seven elements had left exactly one lattice (L7/L10) without a known finite-algebra representation. On 28 August 2026, Chenxiao Tian (Princeton/Peking University) posted a seven-page note exhibiting that lattice as the subgroup interval [SL(2,2)≅S3, PSL(2,64)] (index 43680). The DeMeo–Freese–Jipsen project (GitHub org UniversalAlgebra, repos fin-lat-rep and fin-lat-rep-gap) independently verified this in GAP 4.15.1 by recomputing the interval from Tian's generating matrices, corroborating each lemma of the note (normalizer/centralizer computations, Dickson's classification of maximal subgroups of PSL(2,64), the incidence-count argument), and cross-checking with an independent isomorphism test in the agda-algebras library; they also found a smaller representation as an interval in Sp(6,2) (index 34560) by scanning all 414 tables of marks in GAP's TomLib. This closes the 'one possible exception' from the earlier (pre-2024) DeMeo–Freese–Jipsen work, so with this event every lattice of at most seven elements is now known to be a congruence lattice of a finite algebra — a genuine narrowing of the general open problem's territory, but a restriction (small lattices only) rather than a resolution, so it is classified 'partial' under §3.1's case-vs-variant rule, not 'resolved'. As for AI: no evidence was found that any AI system contributed to the actual mathematics — not to Tian's discovery of the PSL(2,64) representation, not to the group-theoretic verification argument, and not to the Sp(6,2) TomLib scan (performed by a GAP script, tomScan.g). The only AI involvement found is in software engineering: pull requests building the verification/checking infrastructure around this result (and around an unrelated pre-existing bug, algebra B28) carry commit-message credits '🤖 AI-assisted development: Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic)' and 'Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic)', and GitHub Copilot's automated code review flagged bugs in that tooling across several review rounds. This is AI assisting the authors write and debug verification code, not AI producing mathematical content that appears in the result, so ai_role is 'none' per §6.2's instruction that checking, debugging and tooling contributions do not count. This whole episode is extremely recent (weeks old at the time of this research, versus a 26 January 2024 window start) and lives entirely in GitHub issues/PRs of an in-progress manuscript rather than in a published or expert-surveyed venue; I could not find any independent digestion (blog commentary, MathOverflow, journal acceptance) beyond the project's own repositories, so confidence in the permanence/correctness of the classification is medium rather than high, though the verification was done by domain experts (the manuscript's own authors) using two independent methods, which is materially more scrutiny than a bare preprint.
competing_reading: One could argue this event should be rated 'progress' rather than 'partial', on the theory that 'is every finite llattice representable' is functionally an existence/search question similar to the ones §3.1 says a record does not advance merely by narrowing where a counterexample could hide. But that carve-out is for statements like 'are there infinitely many X' where enumerating more X doesn't touch the question; here the case n≤7 is a genuine, exhaustively-defined restriction of the general universally-quantified conjecture ('does every finite lattice L satisfy...'), and settling it removes a specific, previously-open case from the domain — which is exactly what §3.1 defines as a case of the problem meriting 'partial'. A second competing reading is that this should not be recorded at all: the DeMeo-Freese-Jipsen 'one possible exception among ≤7-element lattices' framing is itself a narrower, self-posed sub-problem from their own paper, not a widely-recognized named open problem, so a stickler could call this a 'related' rather than a 'case' of the Wikipedia bullet. I judge it a case because the ≤7-element lattices are a literal, unconditional subset of 'every finite lattice', and DeMeo et al.'s earlier work was itself explicitly working on the Grätzer-Schmidt/Pálfy-Pudlák question restricted by size.
what_would_settle_it: Publication of the updated DeMeo-Freese-Jipsen manuscript (or an arXiv posting of Tian's note itself, which I could not locate independently on arXiv) incorporating this result, and/or independent expert commentary (e.g., a survey, MathOverflow thread, or citation in a later paper) confirming the verification holds up, would move this from a well-verified but insular GitHub-hosted claim toward a fully digested result.

events.what: Tian represents the last unrepresented lattice of at most seven elements (L7/L10) as the subgroup interval [S3, PSL(2,64)]; the DeMeo–Freese–Jipsen project recomputes it in GAP and finds a smaller Sp(6,2) representation

judgement.doubts: The result itself looks sound: it is an explicit subgroup interval that GAP recomputed, and a smaller representation was found independently. The downgrade is about scope, not correctness. The bullet makes a universal claim about all finite lattices. Finishing the census of lattices with at most seven elements shows that finitely many specific lattices are representable, the same pattern as the F4 poset census. It is not a structural class or a parameter range proved by argument. Someone could still read 'all lattices with at most 7 elements' as a size-restricted case (the record's competing reading). If a later pass takes that view, the status would be partial/confirmed. The AI involvement was commit-message credits on verification tooling plus Copilot code review, so ai_role none is correct either way.
